clue.text: Ancient rulers in islands speaking

indicators.note: speaking signals that the islands' name is to be heard rather than spelt, giving a word of the same sound

parts.note: the Faroes are a group of islands in the North Atlantic between Shetland and Iceland

explanation.surface: Some ancient kings are described as talking among island communities.
explanation.walkthrough: The Faroes, a Danish-governed island group, sound just like the title of the kings of ancient Egypt.
explanation.definitionFit: The kings of ancient Egypt bore this title, so they were rulers of antiquity.

clue.text: To share equally is very healthy all round

indicators.note: all round says the word for healthy encircles the letter for very

parts.note: hale means healthy and strong, as in hale and hearty

explanation.surface: Splitting things fairly is said to be thoroughly good for you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all round' puts V inside HALE.
explanation.definitionFit: Dividing something into two equal parts is to split it fairly between two people.

clue.text: Something from Mr Kipling cooked in casserole

indicators.note: cooked suggests the letters of the following words are worked over into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A cake from the Mr Kipling brand has been baked in a casserole dish.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Kipling is a British brand of cakes, which is the misdirection: the definition means the poet Rudyard Kipling, who wrote a poem of this title for Queen Victoria's 1897 jubilee.
explanation.definitionFit: Rudyard Kipling's famous 1897 poem bears this title, so it is a piece of writing by him.

clue.text: Prepare to read book? It has a lot of gaps in it

definitions.text: It has a lot of gaps in it

parts.note: you open a book before reading it
a book is a work, a literary composition

explanation.surface: Getting ready to read a book that seems to have plenty of holes in it.
explanation.walkthrough: Openwork is decorative fabric, metal or lace pierced with a pattern of holes.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacework and fretwork patterns pierced with holes are described by this term, so it is full of gaps.

clue.text: Mild punishment, having heroin close to hand

parts.note: smack is a slang name for heroin
the wrist joins the hand, so something lying there is right next to it

explanation.surface: A light penalty for someone caught with heroin within reach.
explanation.definitionFit: A token reprimand is idiomatically called this, as if a gentle slap were the whole penalty.

clue.text: Top chap's unfriendly manner

parts.note: bod is British slang for a person or chap
ice is coldness of manner, as in an icy reception

explanation.surface: A leading man's frosty demeanour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' looks like an adjective praising the chap but is the definition, a garment for the upper body.
explanation.definitionFit: A close-fitting upper part of a dress is a garment for the torso, a kind of top.

clue.text: Home shortly for our soldiers, bringing spoil

indicators.note: shortly says the word is cut short, losing its final letter

parts.note: Blighty is old British army slang for Britain, home to our soldiers abroad

explanation.surface: Troops coming home on leave bring their loot with them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for our soldiers' tells you to use soldiers' slang for home, Blighty; 'shortly' drops its last letter Y. 'spoil' looks like a noun meaning loot but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To blight something is to ruin or mar it, a synonym for spoil as a verb.

clue.text: Sandwich tossed up for bird

indicators.note: tossed up in a down clue means the word is turned so it reads from the bottom upwards

parts.note: wad is British services slang for a sandwich or bun

explanation.surface: A sandwich thrown into the air for a bird to catch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tossed up' turns WAD round in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A jackdaw is often called by this short name, so it is a kind of bird.

clue.text: Sparkle in court — aces all over the place

indicators.note: all over the place says the letters are scattered and must be put back in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone shines on the tennis court, serving aces everywhere.
explanation.definitionFit: To glitter or flash brilliantly, a literary synonym for sparkling.

clue.text: Cold water excellent to start with — seedlings may need it

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
a loch is a Scottish lake, a body of water

indicators.note: to start with picks only the opening letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: Advice for a gardener: cold water, excellent for beginnings, though seedlings want something more.
explanation.definitionFit: A bell-shaped glass cover protects young plants from frost in a garden.

clue.text: Terrible satire we like

indicators.note: terrible suggests the following words are badly mangled into another order

explanation.surface: We find this satire awful, someone says.
explanation.walkthrough: 'like' here is the filler word of speech, as in 'it was, like, huge'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are hedging fillers in speech meaning so to speak or in a manner of speaking.

clue.text: So-called st James is no more

definitions.meaning: one of the twelve apostles is known as St James the ... to tell him from St James the Great
not as much or not greater in amount

explanation.definitionFit: The apostle is traditionally surnamed this, and the word also means a smaller quantity, not exceeding something.

clue.text: Schoolboy's silly mistake — why?

indicators.note: silly suggests the letters are jumbled foolishly into a new word

explanation.surface: A boy at school asks why he made such a foolish error.
explanation.walkthrough: A pupil of Winchester College, the English public school founded by William of Wykeham, is known by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Pupils of Winchester College, a famous English boarding school, are called by this name.

clue.text: Battle in space, not over supporting planet

indicators.note: in a down entry, supporting means the following letters sit below the planet

parts.note: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun

indicators.note: over signals that the words for space and not are read backwards together

parts.note: room means space, as in room to move
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fight out in space that isn't finished, with forces backing a planet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns the space-and-not pair round as one run, and 'supporting' sets it beneath the planet in this down entry. Marston Moor was a 1644 battle of the English Civil War, fought near York.
explanation.definitionFit: A 1644 English Civil War engagement in Yorkshire, won by Parliamentarians, is known by this name.

clue.text: Assume working across river, there's a small charge here

indicators.note: across means the words for assume and working are laid over the river's letter, enclosing it

parts.note: to posit is to assume or put forward as fact
on means working or functioning, as in a machine being on

explanation.surface: Taking it that you are operating beyond a river, where a small fee is payable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'small charge' suggests a modest fee, but it means a tiny positive electric charge carried by a subatomic particle.
explanation.definitionFit: The antimatter twin of the electron is a particle bearing a minute positive electric charge.

clue.text: Intelligent, like a balancing seal?

definitions.meaning: a circus seal balancing a ball keeps itself perched upon it

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means alert and well informed, and literally describes a performing seal perched upon its ball.

clue.text: Jump back

definitions.meaning: as a verb, to start up or rise suddenly, as a horse does on its hind legs

explanation.definitionFit: A horse rises on its hind legs when startled, and the word also means the hindmost part of anything.

clue.text: Local animals provided, including cross — less stupid than he looks

indicators.note: including says the letter for cross is placed inside the preceding words

parts.note: fauna is the animal life of a particular region
X is the shape of a cross
if means provided that

explanation.surface: The animals hereabouts, so long as a cross-breed is included, are brighter than they appear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'including' sets the cross inside the animals-plus-provided run, splitting the animal word after its third letter. Faux naïf is French for falsely naive.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who only pretends to be innocent or simple is described by this French-derived phrase.

clue.text: Temperature inside star is shock

indicators.note: inside says the temperature letter goes within the word for star

parts.note: the Sun is our nearest star

explanation.surface: The heat at the core of a star is astonishing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' puts T within SUN.
explanation.definitionFit: To stun someone is to daze or astonish them, a synonym for shocking them.

clue.text: Sportsmen are told of fixtures

parts.note: to hear of something is to be told about it
ties are matches or fixtures, as in a cup tie

explanation.surface: Athletes are informed about the forthcoming games.
explanation.walkthrough: A cup tie is a British term for a knockout match between two teams.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearty, outdoorsy athletic types, especially rugby players, are called this in British slang.

clue.text: Take the air?

parts.note: taking the air usually means a stroll outdoors, but read literally it is drawing air into the lungs

explanation.definitionFit: Drawing breath into the lungs literally takes in air, rather than going for a walk.

clue.text: Finally deciding to grow … Cabbages next, of many things to discuss

definitions.text: Cabbages next, of many things to discuss

parts.note: sealing a deal is settling it finally
to wax is to grow, as the moon does

explanation.surface: A line from Lewis Carroll's poem where the Walrus lists topics, with cabbages coming up next.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Walrus and the Carpenter the Walrus says the time has come 'to talk of many things: of shoes and ships and sealing wax, of cabbages and kings'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Carroll's verse the Walrus names it among his topics of talk, just before cabbages.

clue.text: Female and admirer taking turns round common

indicators.note: taking turns round says the pair of words is turned around to read backwards

parts.note: a fan is an admirer

explanation.surface: A woman and her devotee take it in turns to stand a round of drinks at the local.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking turns round' reverses F + FAN, giving the British slang word for tasteless or vulgar.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for tacky or lacking style, much like vulgar.

clue.text: No serious job soldier takes on for kingdom

parts.note: something fun is not a serious matter
GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: A soldier signs up for a light-hearted posting on behalf of his country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kingdom' means a biological kingdom, the top category of living things, not a realm.
explanation.definitionFit: Biologists class mushrooms, moulds and yeasts in their own separate biological kingdom.

clue.text: Finished with lamb once, I get beef

parts.note: past means over or finished
a ram was once a lamb, before it grew up
taken as written

explanation.surface: Having had enough lamb, I'll have beef instead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beef' looks like a meat being chosen, and it is: a seasoned smoked beef, also popular in delis.
explanation.definitionFit: This spiced, smoked cured meat is made from beef brisket.

clue.text: Container, small but bottomless

indicators.note: bottomless in a down entry means the final letter at the foot of the word is taken away

parts.note: tiny means very small

explanation.surface: A box that is little and has no base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bottomless' drops Y from TINY.
explanation.definitionFit: A metal can or box is a common receptacle for food.

clue.text: Quantity of horse, maybe

parts.note: in casual speech of is often slurred to a, as in cuppa for cup of tea or lotsa for lots of
a horse is one example of a mount, an animal ridden; maybe signals the example

explanation.surface: Someone asks how much horse there might be on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a question of how much horse there is, but it splits as A MOUNT, with 'of' giving A as in colloquial cuppa.
explanation.definitionFit: A total or sum is a measure of how much of something there is.

clue.text: Shot by good weapon

parts.note: a lance is a long spear carried by a knight

explanation.surface: Struck down by a fine weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' looks like 'fired at', but a glance is a cricket stroke deflecting the ball fine with the bat.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket, a deflecting stroke off the face of the bat is a kind of batting stroke.

clue.text: Stern guard from Welsh train company?

parts.note: Taff is a nickname for a Welshman, from the River Taff in Cardiff
rail suggests a railway operator, with the question mark admitting the stretch

explanation.surface: A protective rail made by a Welsh railway firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stern' looks like an adjective for a strict guard, but it is the rear of a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A rail around the stern of a ship guards those on deck there.
